item.title: Prediction Markets and Betting on Elections
item.description:
Compulsive Behaviors

Prediction Markets and Betting on Elections

There can be heavy costs to wagering on elections.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Prediction markets allow people over the age of 18 to trade event contracts.
  • Prediction markets may contribute to growing gambling-related harms.
  • Betting on elections can be a threat to individuals and to democracy.

Federal law prohibits online gambling platforms such as DraftKings or FanDuel from wagers on election outcomes. On the prediction markets of Kalshi and Polymarket, a person can buy an event contract on an election. This election cycle, nearly $1.9 billion has been traded on these markets.

What's the difference between online betting and prediction markets?

Both online gambling platforms and prediction markets involve future events. What’s the difference between wagers and event contracts? That may be a distinction in search of a difference. Regardless, the effects of these platforms and markets on individuals, our elections, and democracy matter enormously.

With online betting, a person may place a wager on the outcome of a sports event, a card game, or just about anything else but an election. If a person has a winning bet, the online platform, a.k.a. the house, must pay out. The house has an interest in a particular outcome. To gamble legally online, a person must be at least 21 years old.

In a prediction market, participants buy event contracts about the outcome of future events, which might include sports, military operations, election outcomes, and when a celebrity couple will get married. Prediction markets set prices by probabilities. An event contract selling for $.25 that the local football team will win the day’s game implies there is a 25 percent likelihood of the team winning. Purchasing an event contract is a financial transaction and not a wager. Participants in a prediction market trade directly with the other participants. The market is neutral on the outcome. Kalshi charges a fee for each transaction, but they do not pay out like the house does with gambling. This is the crux of the argument that prediction markets are not a form of online betting. To buy event contracts, a person must be at least 18 years old.

Tomato, tomahto. I believe that prediction markets are online betting by another name. This form of online gambling poses significant risks to individuals and to our democracy. I have four concerns that weave together.

The age of bettors

Nearly 75 percent of Kalshi’s event contracts involve sports. It is young men who are fueling the online betting and purchase of event contracts. The younger a person is when he starts betting, the greater the likelihood of developing a problem with gambling and experiencing gambling-related harm. This may begin with people visiting the platforms more often and spending increasing amounts of time there. Dynamic pricing in the prediction market makes that more likely. When new information is available, public sentiment shifts, or there are changes in risk tolerance, the price of the event contract shifts. These pricing changes keep bettors tethered to the platform and making trades with each other.

Cognitive offloading

The price of an event contract is the result of artificial intelligence (AI) crunching massive amounts of data. Most bettors just look at the results of the crunching, follow those results, and trade their contracts repeatedly. Following along because AI has indicated probabilities is a new version of the bandwagon fallacy. Old-school bandwagon fallacy involves the assertion that a claim is true because the majority of people believe it is true, which prompts more people to hop on the bandwagon. AI now functions as the supermajority for most people, which makes individuals less willing and even able to seek their own evidence and argument.

Gamification of our civic duty

For those young people who grew up playing video games, online gambling sites will be familiar as entertainment or excitement. Prediction markets allow people to bet on the outcomes of elections as if they were games. Free and fair elections are the backbone of a democracy. Now they are viewed as akin to a sporting event. The stakes are enormously high with elections; their consequences extend for years. Voting affords the opportunity for people to make their voices heard and their preferences known. Young people arguably have the greatest stake in elections because they will have to live with the consequences for longer periods of time. Choosing candidates and buying event contracts based on probabilities of their winning as opposed to their characters or their platforms is not genuine voter engagement.

Individualism and moral callousness

Betting on elections becomes a matter of an individual’s personal gain from an election outcome. It telescopes a person’s interest in an election to the probability of that person winning a bet. Winning the bet becomes more important than the consequences of the election. I am not naïve to assume that personal interest hasn’t governed people’s voting patterns, but these bets radically change the calculus. A person’s vote will follow the bet. This makes it less likely that people would vote for something beyond their self-interest, such as the well-being of others or the common good.

Prediction markets can harm individuals, the common good, and even democracy itself.

item.title: Surviving Holiday Family Gatherings
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Surviving Holiday Family Gatherings

Adult children of emotionally abusive families may struggle at holiday gatherings.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • You have more power than you realize. Set limits and boundaries, and practice standing up for yourself.
  • There are specific ways to take care of yourself so you don't end up feeling revictimized.
  • Consider how you may be contributing to the family drama.
  • Know that you can always leave—the room or the house—if you feel overwhelmed or attacked.

Adult children of emotionally abusive families may dread spending time with their family, especially during the holidays. If this applies to you, instead of feeling constantly victimized by family members during holiday gatherings, try the following suggestions that may help you feel more in control of what occurs.

  1. The most important thing to do is to remember that holidays bring back memories of when you were a child, when you had no control over what happened to you. It is important to remind yourself that you are now an adult, and as such, you have a lot more say in terms of creating your holiday experience.
  2. Take good care of yourself by getting plenty of sleep the night before a visit. If you find yourself getting anxious, take steps to calm yourself down by listening to calm music, taking a walk or run, or writing your feelings down in a journal.
  3. Consider staying at a hotel instead of a family member’s house. If this is the home you were raised in, the house itself can become a trigger, reminding you of past traumatic events. Also, if you stay at a hotel, you will have a place to escape to if you become overwhelmed.
  4. Instead of constantly feeling victimized by the behavior of other family members, take a close look at what you may be doing to contribute to the family drama. For example, do you have a tendency to compete with your siblings for your parents’ attention? If so, you can eliminate feeling hurt by opting out of the competition. For instance, instead of focusing your attention on what is going on between your parents and your siblings, focus instead on your spouse and your children.
  5. If you are holding on to a lot of anger toward a family member, consider writing an “anger letter” in which you write down all the reasons you are angry with this person—all the things they have done to hurt you. Don’t censor yourself; write down everything you are feeling. You are not going to send this letter, so it is not going to hurt your family member. It is just an exercise in releasing pent-up anger so that it will be less likely to spill out during the gathering.
  6. Prepare for your visit by creating a “triggers” list, a list of situations that remind you of past childhood hurts or traumas. Then, when you become upset, ask yourself if you have been triggered. If you have been, bring yourself back to the present by taking some deep breaths, feeling your feet on the ground, or picking a color and looking around the room to find objects that are that color.
  7. If you were emotionally, physically, or sexually abused by a sibling or a parent when you were growing up and this family member continues to bully, challenge, or abuse you, consider whether it is safe to be around them. You aren’t being a wimp or a weakling because you freeze in their presence. You aren’t being a coward because you find that you can’t speak up for yourself. These are normal reactions to having been traumatized. Either choose to opt out of any family gathering where you will be exposed to this person or practice standing up to them. You will become more self-confident and feel more empowered every time you speak up.
  8. If one or more family members have an alcohol or drug problem, avoid drinking or taking drugs around them (yes, including marijuana). This is especially true if you’ve noticed that family arguments and drama usually occur after everyone has been partaking.
  9. If you know or suspect that a family member suffers from a personality disorder such as borderline personality disorder (BPD), narcissistic personality disorder (NPD), or another type of mental illness, don’t expect them to change their behavior without extensive therapy. Instead, learn all you can about their condition. The more you understand them, the better able you will be to cope with their behavior. Also, know what you are walking into and prepare yourself for their hurtful, challenging, or abusive behavior. Instead of reacting by getting angry with them or telling them how wrong they are, simply excuse yourself and leave their presence, whether it means leaving the room or leaving the house.
  10. Set clear boundaries when it comes to how family members can treat you and your children (for example, “you can’t yell at my kids”). Personal limits and boundaries are not about controlling other people’s behavior but are actually an example of taking care of yourself. For instance, unacceptable behavior from a BPD or NPD family member can include: “lashing out” at you when they are triggered, verbally abusing you with name-calling, and talking negatively about you with other family members behind your back. If a family member crosses your boundaries, protect your children and be a positive role model for them by taking them out of the presence of the offending family member. You don’t have to create a big scene, just quietly pack up your things and go.

Hopefully, the above suggestions will help you take care of yourself when you are in your parent’s, sibling’s, or other abusive family member’s presence, but if you find that you aren’t able to follow these recommendations, please don’t chastise yourself or think of yourself as weak. Instead, treat yourself with self-compassion and remember that you sustained a great deal of damage growing up in your emotionally abusive household, and this damage may still be preventing you from acting on your own behalf. Give yourself credit for the changes you have been able to make and trust that by continuing in your efforts to heal, you will eventually feel empowered enough to stand up for yourself and take care of yourself in the ways you deserve.

And remember: You may feel obligated to spend the holidays with your family, but you have an even more important obligation to protect yourself and your children from dangerous and abusive family members.

item.title: Seeking Spiritual Friendship on the Path to Enlightenment
item.description:
Friends

Seeking Spiritual Friendship on the Path to Enlightenment

How spiritual allies support us on our journey.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • We benefit and enlarge our inner resources with a spiritual companion.
  • Spiritual friendships challenge ego, nurturing generosity, humility, and loving-kindness.
  • Our circle of friends can include someone who joins us on our spiritual path.

People over the centuries have referred to spiritual companionship and assistance as a relationship with a “spiritual friend.” The Gaelic word anamchara refers to the spiritual friend as a “soul-friend.” A soul-friend is an assisting force on our journey. This is the reliable confidant with whom we can share our innermost spiritual conundrums, visions, and realizations.

As St. Aelred (1111-1167), the Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx Abbey in medieval England, wrote in On Spiritual Friendship: “It is no small consolation in this life to have someone who can unite with you in an intimate affection and the embrace of a holy love. Someone in whom your spirit can rest, to whom you can pour out your soul, to whose pleasant exchanges, as to soothing songs, you can fly in sorrow. To the dear breast of whose friendship, amidst the many troubles of the world, you can safely retire. A person who can shed tears with you in your worries, be happy with you when things go well, search out with you the answers to your problems, whom with the ties of charity you can lead into the depths of your heart. A person who, though absent in body, is yet present in spirit, where heart to heart you can talk to him, where the sweetness of the Spirit flows between you, where you so join yourself and cleave to him that soul mingles with soul and two become one.”

In Buddhism we find the idea of Kalyana-mittata, “virtuous friendship.” The spiritual friends support one another’s practice with candidness, wisdom, and trustworthiness. In the Upaddha Sutta, Buddha explained to Ananda, his disciple, cousin, and friend, that such spiritual companionship can be considered the whole of the Dharma as the “holy life.” Buddha went on to say that when we have Kalyana-mittata in place with friends, they cheer and encourage us on the path, and when our friend is Buddha, we are fully freed from suffering. In the Dighajanu Sutta, Buddha says that when a practitioner is committed to dialogue with a variety of upstanding people, he learns to imitate their commitment to the Dharma, their compassion, their discerning wisdom. They have become allies of enlightenment to one another.

Another text, the Anguttara Nikaya, lists the qualities of a monastic spiritual friend: he is amiable, venerable, able to give good counsel, patient in listening, respectful, capable of speaking in depth about the Dharma, and serious enough to share on a depth level. A teacher is a prime example of what is required in spiritual friendship. He, she, or they offer guidance, challenges, comfort, and cheer on the path to virtue and awakening—all the scaffolding of authentic support. A support group, a faith community, or a sangha, a coterie of practitioners of Buddhism, are examples.

Peer companionship is certainly valuable on the spiritual path. Our spiritual practice and our psychological health are enlivened when we have a trusted friend to whom we can speak openly about ourselves. This will not be the “friend” who supports and cheers our ego and its inflation—a narcissistic style of alliance. The ally of our higher Self supports our journey toward generosity, humility, enlightenment, and loving-kindness. This ally warns and saves us from what in Buddhism are called the three poisons: greed, hate, and the illusion of separateness. These are descriptors of the inflated ego at its worst. Spiritual friends will be the ones who show and lead us from greed to generosity, from hate to love, and from ignorance to wisdom.

“Ubuntu” is an African term meaning “humanity toward others.” It is also translated as “I am because you are” or “I am what I am because of who we all are.” Ubuntu tells us that all beings can be allies, contributing to our becoming what we can best be in this moment. Ubuntu is also a spiritual calling to reach out to and care about all beings as relatives in the family of humanity. Ubuntu transcends race and creed. All diversity becomes, or rather is, only one reality, just what the Buddhas and mystics in all traditions came to realize. We feel an intense, ineradicable sense of belonging and we pass on to others that same joyous sense. We remind ourselves that we are not stand-alone beings; we exist only with everyone else, the solidarity that Thich Nhat Hanh calls “inter-being.”

We notice unanimous agreement among the assisting-counseling forces in all times and traditions: We can be allies to one another only if there are no boundaries to our assisting outreach. Indeed, such boundaries are really barriers. The wise, courageous assisting forces in all traditions have made the journey from insulation to universal embrace. They see diversity as a path to unity. Their caring, committed connection has no frontier.

"We never are deserted quite."

—Christopher Smart, “On a Bed of Guernsey Lilies”

Adapted from By Your Side: How to Find Soulful Allies and Become One to Others (Shambhala, 2024)

item.title: Can Finding Perfection Backfire?
item.description:
Awe

Can Finding Perfection Backfire?

Personal Perspective: For sensitive people, extreme beauty may be disturbing.

Posted November 3, 2026

Things were starting to feel rather boring at home—the same old places, the same old food, the same old sunsets. I’ve learned to be very wary of boredom, because it’s a close cousin to one of my least favorite symptoms of depression: anhedonia. Anhedonia is the inability to experience pleasure; things that used to give you pleasure (that amazing Malibu sunset, for example) no longer move you the same way.

It was clearly time to get away from my usual haunts. I needed a startle, an awakening, something that would reset my pleasure circuits so life didn’t feel so humdrum. Simply put, I needed a good healthy dose of awe.

Travel is one of the best ways I know to stoke the wonder inside me. Fortunately, my partner, Colin, was up for it. We thought and thought about where to go, and then, one day, I just knew. I wanted rejuvenation? I wanted rebirth? Then why not go to the very heart of it?

Why not relive the Renaissance?

That meant, of course, heading to Florence. Historians credit Florence as the birthplace of Europe’s revivification after the Middle Ages, and it sounded simply ideal: museums overflowing with masterpieces, architecture so beautiful it could take one’s breath away. Literally. The so-called “Stendhal syndrome” originated there, when in 1817 French author Stendhal took one look at the Basilica of Santa Croce and fainted, overwhelmed by its magnificence.

I certainly wasn’t hoping to faint dead away, but to be so transported by beauty sounded heavenly. It sounded exactly like the cure I was seeking.

My anticipation grew with each passing day, until the trip was practically all I could think about. Colin and I were especially looking forward to seeing Michelangelo’s famous statue of David. At very long last, we found ourselves standing outside the Galleria dell’Accademia. There was a long line to get in, but what did it matter? David awaited.

When the guards started admitting people, there was some jostling, but eventually the rooms grew wider and the crowd, although still very much a crowd, grew thinner. I let go of Colin’s hand to search through my purse for my camera. When I found it and looked around for him, I was so astonished I nearly dropped my phone. There, illuminating Colin’s face, was the very sensation I had traveled so far for and hoped so much to find: awe.

I followed his gaze, and then I saw it, too: Michelangelo’s David. He dominated the room and dwarfed the tourists scrambling to capture his image. They encircled him, but he remained untouched, his smooth white marble immune to their adoration. I marveled at his potent form, every sinew of his body taut and ready for battle, his gaze resolute and unwavering. He stood forever on the edge of glory.

No, dear reader, I didn’t faint—although a pregnant woman next to me grew dizzy and had to be helped to a seat by a guard. The crowd, which had been so lively outside, was strangely quiet, as if in church. And it did feel like a sacred space. I knew, without being able to articulate it at the time, that I was in the presence of something holy, a talent so astounding that only a higher power could bestow it.

In a word, I’d seen perfection.

And contrary to everything I had expected, it didn’t instantly cure my discontent. I felt very strange—disconnected from my surroundings, and deeply disturbed. What was going on? I didn’t know how to explain my feelings to Colin, because I didn’t really understand them myself. All I knew was that compared to David, everything else seemed plebeian.

We went back to our hotel. There were frescoes on the walls and ceiling of our room that I’d delighted in just a few hours before. But now, I was only aware of their flaws. And worse yet, I was aware of mine. For all my artistic ambitions, I’d never create anything even remotely approaching a David.

I couldn’t help but wonder what other artists had felt in the face of incomparable beauty—and I wasn’t surprised by what I found out. Camus summed it up: “Beauty is unbearable, drives us to despair, offering us for a minute the glimpse of an eternity that we should like to stretch out over the whole of time.”

Exactly. So now what was I going to do, knowing that the rest of life would never reach the level of perfection I’d just witnessed?

“Let’s go to lunch,” Colin said, always the pragmatist. “You’ll feel better after you eat.”

A half-hour later, I sat in front of a large, steaming bowl of fusilli al pesto and toyed with my fork. I was sick of being so damned sensitive. Why couldn’t I just be moved by perfection, and let it go?

Then I took a bite of my fusilli. Oh my God, it was the most delicious thing I’d ever tasted. The pasta was just firm enough, the pesto fragrant and slightly sweet, with a teasing, subtle undertone of garlic. I looked up at Colin and smiled. He smiled back—relieved, no doubt, that I wasn’t moping anymore.

So maybe I couldn’t be perfect. Maybe I was meant to be like Salieri in Amadeus, fated to simply appreciate perfection. That didn’t mean I had to be miserable. That afternoon in Florence, sitting across from the love of my life, a perfect moment came and went, and I was there to know it.

item.title: Why It's Difficult to Be a Good Leader
item.description:
Leadership

Why It's Difficult to Be a Good Leader

Effective leaders have to continually navigate multiple polarities.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Polarities are opposing goals that fall at either end of a continuum, such as autonomy and supervision.
  • Polarities create tensions leaders must navigate; poor management of polarities can affect leadership quality.
  • Being explicit about relevant polarities can benefit both leaders and followers.

When I conduct a workshop or extended program on leadership development, I often start by asking participants to identify the various characteristics of “good leaders.” Regardless of the audience, their lists are typically similar. In other words, the characteristics that define good leaders are not a secret, and there is general agreement as to what those characteristics are. I then follow with a question: “If this isn’t a secret, why don’t we see more actual leaders who exhibit these characteristics?”

Of course there are several viable answers to that question, but one important answer that gets overlooked is polarities that are inherent in leadership within an organization. What’s a polarity? Imagine a continuum, anchored at each end by a competing goal. As you invest more in reaching one of the goals, it’s like a pendulum swinging toward that end of the continuum, and you risk failing to reach the other goal. That is a polarity, and the trick is to continually and intentionally manage where you are on the continuum, recognizing that focusing more at one end tends to starve achievement of the goal at the other end.

As an example, a common polarity that many employed individuals face is the work-family polarity. The more time and energy devoted to work tends to result in negligence of one’s family, and vice versa. In a sense, “work-life balance” implies maintaining a midpoint position on the continuum. In reality, work or family often receives more than 50 percent of one’s time and energy due to what is needed in each domain at the time. Perhaps the ultimate goal of “life success” rests on not neglecting work or family for too long.

What about leaders in organizational settings? They commonly face a number of polarities, including these:

  • The need to motivate people while holding them accountable
  • The need to offer critical feedback while building trust
  • The need to make unpopular decisions while strengthening relationships
  • The need to deliver immediate results while developing people for the future
  • The need to promote productivity while protecting people from burnout
  • The need to focus on the big picture while remaining aware of life in the trenches
  • The need to be transparent while maintaining people’s respect and trust
  • The need to give people autonomy while staying close enough to the work to catch problems early

I imagine there are additional polarities, and perhaps some that are specific to each setting, but managing even this set listed here represents a monumental achievement. Leaders frequently notice a deficit in some area, perhaps followers regularly working in ways that do not align with the organization’s priorities. We might say that the leader’s pendulum had swung too far toward allowing autonomy. Because it’s now a problem, the unfortunate tendency is to swing too far in the other direction. In this case, the leader may take a heavy hands-on approach, which ends up frustrating followers as they complain of being micromanaged.

Just as leaders commonly focus on instances where a pendulum swung too far in one direction within the polarity, followers do as well. In the example of too much autonomy, at least some followers likely felt as though they did not receive enough direction or supervision. Just like Goldilocks and the Three Bears, the trick is finding and maintaining the area within the polarity that feels “just right.” Unfortunately, what constitutes “just right” varies across individuals.

So what can leaders do? Identify the prominent polarities they must navigate, and work on resisting the temptation to swing too far in one direction when trying to rectify a situation in which the other end of the continuum had been overly emphasized. I also suggest being explicit in explaining to followers the concept of polarities and the inherent tension the leader faces in each one. The hope is that followers begin to notice when a polarity is becoming out of balance and can alert leadership.

Perhaps you’re not a leader, and instead feel as though you are at the mercy of polarities over which you have little (if any) control. In that case, you now know about polarities and have that construct with which to better understand at least some of the problems you encounter at work. That knowledge doesn’t remove the negative effects of being too far toward one end of a continuum, but hopefully it provides the ability to recognize that leaders face difficult polarities. Because leaders frequently have not heard of the concept and the dynamic that polarities explain, it may be helpful for you to share this post with the leaders you think may benefit from it.

item.title: The Loneliness Trap
item.description:
Happiness

The Loneliness Trap

Why your Amazon Cart doesn’t bring you happiness.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • The secret to happiness lies in what we share, not what we buy.
  • Prioritize doing activities you enjoy in person with people you care about rather than buying objects.
  • Spend time with the people you love, or could love if you were to get to know them better.

With unyielding inflation, economic uncertainty, and geopolitical friction sending collective anxiety levels higher and higher, many of us now consider genuine contentment an unaffordable luxury. Yet many decades of history serve as reminders that even amidst tremendous upheaval, human joy has never depended on what you can buy or external calm.

In this challenging environment, most of us want what we’ve always wanted: to be genuinely happy. Yet we are not willing to do what it takes to become happy.

The Miner’s Secret: How a 1938 Coal Worker Found Contentment in a World on Fire

A study from almost a century ago of the residents of the Northern English town of Bolton shows us the severe effects of not carving out time for our loved ones, a decision that most of us make every day. In the year my father was born, just over 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) to the east in Hungary, 1938—and then again in 2014—the residents of Bolton were asked what made them happy.

The most common ingredients of happiness among responses spanning 78 years were economic security and personal relationships, which were often tied together. Little mention was made of external events.

Joseph Roberts, a miner, despite answering the survey in 1938 when the threat of Hitler loomed large—the Nazi leader had already occupied Austria and parts of what was then Czechoslovakia—shared that what made him happy was returning from a day of hard work and spending time with his family.

“I see my kiddies and wife I am happy,” shared the miner. “When I am washed and romp with my kiddies, and when it is weekend and I tip up my humble wage and share with my wife in doling it out and we find we can manage another week we are happy. I am in regular work although it is hard and dangerous but I am happy because I have a contented mind.”

The Garden in Which Happiness Grows

I am guessing you would agree that happiness is a seed you must grow in your life. Yet what most people do not understand is that you can’t grow your happiness alone; you can only do so with the help of others.

Shared experiences and meaningful relationships create more lasting happiness than material possessions.
Source: Felix Rostig / Unsplash

Since you cannot grow your happiness alone, it must also be true that happiness is a seed that grows in the gardens of others. How does this work?

We all seek happiness yet find it elusive. The reason is that most of us do not realize that one of the best ways to experience happiness is to help others experience it.

Plato understood this well. “Caring for the happiness of others,” observed the Greek philosopher over 2,500 years ago, “we find our own.”

Research also bears this out. Not only do people feel even more appreciated, happy, and connected to us than we expect them to when we give to them, but we also counterintuitively often benefit, as psychologists Sonja Lyubomirsky and Harry Reis note in their book How to Feel Loved, even more than they do.

I was reminded of this truth last month, when I spent nine days in a small town in rural Kenya where I had lived and worked as a Peace Corps volunteer 35 years earlier. Facilitating a pro bono leadership conference for rural primary and secondary school leaders and supporting five Kenyan women educators in teaching a women’s empowerment program for single mothers in one of Kenya’s most impoverished regions, I was struck by how happy I felt connecting with the people around me.

Returning to my comparatively more hermetic life of writing, researching, and teaching in Rome has been a jolt to my system; yet the memories remain and bring peace. In the end, I am like everyone else I’ve ever met in the world: traveling on an eternal search for connection and meaning.

Wish for Their Happiness

Following the Italian way of expressing love, when you tell the other person “Ti voglio bene” (which means “I wish for your happiness”), you offer them the seed of happiness to plant in their own garden. You give them your support to grow in the way they desire, toward their own goals and values, or “to become,” as the former president of the American Psychological Association and the father of client-centered therapy, Carl Rogers, once wrote.

If the seed flourishes and becomes the flower of happiness, the other person may or may not bring you this flower one day. Sound risky? It may be; yet it’s the only way you will ever have the experience of seeing this flower in full bloom.

In other words, interconnectedness is the only path that will enable you to experience and sustain happiness throughout your life.

“Sounds good, Mr. Idealistic Author,” you may be thinking. “But how do I make daily decisions that will bring this interconnectedness into my life?”

If you want a more interconnected life, you will first have to ask yourself some tough questions about your daily decisions, right down to whether you should spend your time today ordering another gadget on Amazon or going hiking with a friend. Let’s consider this choice.

Experiences Versus Objects

What do you think will bring you more happiness—an Amazon delivery or going on a hike with a friend? A study by Amit Kumar of the University of Texas has found that once you have a base level of financial resources, experiences rather than objects are the drivers of happiness.

Why? Experiences (“doing” something such as going to a meditation retreat or on a bicycle ride or to a restaurant or a concert) are more often shared, while objects (“owning” something such as a new shirt or book) are most often enjoyed alone.

In the end, the love we’ve shared with others is all we take with us. “All that we love deeply,” Helen Keller sagely observed, “becomes a part of us.” This is why experiences, which facilitate the sharing of love, produce much more long-term happiness than objects.

Bring It Back Home

How, then, can you usher more happiness back into your life? Prioritize doing activities you enjoy in person with people you care about rather than buying objects to enjoy by your lonesome.

Just as you pursue objects to purchase and yet Prime shipping does not drop happiness at your doorstep, you also pursue social information about the people in your social network. As I write in my book Screened In, this search—like buying objects—does not bring the social connection that is the purveyor of genuine happiness into your life.

In sum, then, stop texting and call, go out with, see, visit, meet—in short, spend time with other, values-congruent people as often as you can.

Genuine happiness grows when we prioritize face-to-face connections with the people who matter most.
Source: Tyson / Unsplash

In other words: Just. Connect. In person. In real time.

Spend time with the people you love, or could love if you were to get to know them better. Then happiness will cease to be a distant stranger and will become a part of your life again.

item.title: Navigating the Holidays When You're Estranged From Family
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Navigating the Holidays When You're Estranged From Family

Practical ways to cope when you've cut ties with a parent or family member.

Posted November 3, 2026

Source: Pexels/instasky

Knowing you had to cut ties with your parent to protect yourself doesn't make the holidays any easier. It's normal to miss having a family to celebrate with, feel guilty about not being together, or dread questions about why you're not seeing your parents. Even when you know you've made the right decision, the holidays can bring up feelings you thought you'd worked through.

Here's how to navigate the season in a way that protects your well-being and helps you regain some joy.

Why Holidays Are So Hard When You're Estranged

For many adult children of dysfunctional parents, holidays can be painful reminders of both your current reality and what you've lost. You may find yourself grieving the parent you're estranged from, but also the parent you always wished you'd had. It's completely natural to feel confused or upset; part of you may still long for a nurturing, loving connection, while another part knows that staying in a toxic relationship would only cause more pain.

Holidays can amplify these feelings because they're built around an idealized version of family that's never been your reality. You may feel pressure to attend gatherings that feel unsafe, or you may be flooded with painful memories when everyone around you seems to be celebrating. The goal is to learn to tolerate such feelings, knowing that they will lessen, and to treat yourself with compassion.

Should You Attend Holiday Gatherings?

The first decision is whether to attend family events at all. This is always a choice, even when it doesn't feel like one. Choosing not to attend a gathering when your estranged parent will be there isn’t necessarily a sign of avoidance but of maintaining a boundary. If you do choose to attend, it should be because it genuinely serves you—and not because of guilt, obligation, or pressure from others.

Take time to weigh your options. Ask yourself: What's the emotional cost of attending? What do you hope to gain—and is it realistic? And will being there require you to compromise your boundaries or safety? (For people with abusive or toxic parents, skipping a holiday gathering may be the healthiest decision.)

How to Prepare for Holidays When You're Estranged

Once you've made your decision, preparation can help you avoid reactive choices in an already emotional situation. Anxiety can build for days or weeks before a difficult holiday, so don't wait until the day arrives to think through your approach.

If you're not attending: Resist the pull to leave the day unstructured. A completely open day can intensify rumination and sadness. Plan something intentional that gives you something grounded to move toward.

If you're attending: Go in with a clear plan so you feel more grounded and in control.

  • Decide in advance how long you'll stay. Knowing you can leave at a specific time reduces the feeling of being trapped.
  • Identify your boundaries before you're in the room—which topics are off-limits, which behavior you won't engage with, and how you'll handle pressure from others about your estrangement.
  • Anticipate their reaction. They might ignore you, act overly affectionate, or try to corner you. Planning your response now prevents you from being caught off guard later.
  • Decide how much contact feels right. You don't have to choose between a long talk and total silence. A simple nod or a "hello" honors your boundaries without making a scene.
  • Bring a support person, if possible.
  • Take breaks. Step outside or find a quiet space to regroup as needed.
  • Have an exit strategy. Know ahead of time when and how you'll leave if the situation becomes overwhelming.

Estrangement invites you to rethink what holidays can look like. You don't have to organize your life around traditions that cause pain; giving yourself permission to step away is progress in itself.

Think creatively about how you want to spend the holiday. Start new traditions, volunteer, or do something you genuinely enjoy but rarely make time for—a hike, a movie, or a good book. It's also completely fine to use the time to rest, reflect, practice self-care, do chores, or pursue hobbies. There are no rules: How you spend the day is completely up to you, whether that means making new meaning out of the holiday or simply getting through it in whatever way feels manageable.

Coping Strategies for Holidays When You're Estranged

Holidays can be emotionally draining, regardless of what you decide to do. In my book, Cutting Ties with Your Parents, I share these strategies for getting through the season:

  • Acknowledge your feelings and find healthy outlets for them.
  • Lean on others for strength and comfort, whether through professional support or friendships.
  • Increase self-care before and after the holiday. I call this a “self-care sandwich.”
  • Avoid social media or anything that stirs up strong negative emotions.
  • Give yourself permission to celebrate differently or not at all.
  • Spend time with others who are also without family.
  • Make a flexible plan for the day so you aren't left with unstructured time, which can invite rumination and sorrow.

Journaling is one of the most effective tools for working through complicated emotions; it slows your thinking and brings clarity. Try reflecting on questions like, What am I grieving today? What do I wish I'd received from my parents that I didn't? and What do I need right now, and how can I give it to myself?

If anxiety or distressing memories surface, try a grounding exercise, deep breathing, or a guided meditation to help interrupt the stress response.

Final Thoughts

Estrangement can’t erase the hurt you've experienced, but it can create space for healing. With each holiday you navigate, you may build more clarity about who you are, what you need, and what matters most to you. With practice, you’ll move from simply surviving the season to building traditions and relationships that feel safer, healthier, and more joyful.

item.title: Beyond Bars and Into Being
item.description:
Trauma

Beyond Bars and Into Being

How creative arts can help improve outcomes for formerly incarcerated people.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Many re-entry programs focus on employment and housing but overlook the lasting trauma incarceration produces.
  • Creative work may help people rebuild identity, emotional control, and a sense of purpose after incarceration.
  • Controlled trials suggest arts therapies in forensic care may ease symptoms and improve functioning.

By Maya Lakshman, MPH

Midway through the 2024 film "Sing Sing," a group of men rehearses a play in a classroom at a maximum-security prison in New York (Kwedar, 2024). Some of the actors learned their craft while they were incarcerated. They are alumni of Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA), the theater program the film portrays, and on screen they play versions of themselves.

RTA makes a striking claim about what happens after its participants go home: only around 5% return to prison (ABC7 New York, 2022). Nationally, 27% of people released from prison are reincarcerated within three years, down from 35% for those released in 2008 (Council of State Governments [CSG] Justice Center, 2024). The national figure is moving in the right direction. RTA’s figure suggests the arts may be reaching people in ways standard rehabilitation misses.

One possibility is that creative engagement addresses barriers conventional re-entry programs tend to overlook: trauma, a disrupted sense of self, and strained emotional capacity. The idea is promising, and the research behind it is still young.

What Prison Leaves Behind

The past two decades have brought new investment in re-entry, including the Second Chance Act of 2008, which funded education, mental health care, and substance use treatment for people leaving prison (CSG Justice Center, 2024). Attending to these needs is valuable; however, far less attention goes to what years inside do to a person’s mind and body. “The legal system, and incarceration more specifically, produces a legacy of intergenerational trauma and health harms,” says Dr. Rebecca Fix, an Assistant Professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Instead of addressing the traumatic circumstances that led many to incarceration, prisons exacerbate those harms.”

In a study of about 4,000 incarcerated men, 44.7% reported physical trauma in childhood (Wolff & Shi, 2012). Current rates of post-traumatic stress disorder are roughly five times more common among men in prison than in the general population, and about eight times more common among women (Baranyi et al., 2018). Experiences in prison typically perpetuate this trauma and distress. Victimization, solitary confinement, and coercion experienced in prison are each associated with PTSD (Piper & Berle, 2019).

Among people released after long sentences, researchers have identified a lasting cluster of symptoms that includes chronic distrust, difficulty making decisions, and trouble sustaining relationships (Liem & Kunst, 2013). Poet Reginald Dwayne Betts was incarcerated at 16 and spent 14 months in solitary confinement. His collection Felon traces how that time follows a person long after release (Betts, 2019). These are the very capacities people need to rebuild their lives at home, work, and in their families, and most re-entry services do little to restore them.

Rebuilding Through the Arts

Coming home after prison means building a new story about who one is, one in which a person sees themselves as capable, creative, and worthy of a future (Maruna, 2001). Creative work offers a place to start writing that story (Fleetwood, 2020). For example, Jimmy Santiago Baca (2001) entered prison unable to read and taught himself to read and write there, emerging as a poet. Shaka Senghor (2016), who spent seven of his 19 years in prison in solitary confinement, credits literature and self-examination with helping him confront his past.

Making art engages the body and the senses along with language. In one small study of adults outside prison, 45 minutes of art-making lowered levels of the stress hormone cortisol in about three-quarters of participants (Kaimal et al., 2016). In another study, dance movement therapy lowered depression scores by 72% in 12 weeks (Jeong et al., 2005).

Theater and writing give people a place to try on a new identity. On stage, someone the system calls an inmate becomes an actor, a writer, a member of an ensemble, and an audience watches that change happen. Narrative identity research links redemptive life stories to well-being (McAdams & McLean, 2013), and performance may be one way to rehearse such a story out loud (Maruna, 2001). Ashley Lucas (2020), former director of the Prison Creative Arts Project, draws on years of directing theater in prisons to describe how performance builds community and hope in settings designed to strip both away. In Baltimore, Center Stage launched a year-long theater program in 2024 with young people held at the city’s Juvenile Justice Center (Baltimore Center Stage, n.d.). Stella Adler Studio of Acting has been partnering with the Rikers Island Correctional Facility since 2014. Every week across the year, a cadre of trained artists – including teachers, writers, voice and speech experts, movement coaches and directors – visit multiple facilities to reach hundreds of inmates annually. Ensemble work asks for turn-taking, negotiation, and impulse control, too. In an evaluation of California prison arts programs, participants reported gains in emotional control, time management, and self-confidence, and disciplinary reports fell (Brewster, 2014).

An evaluation of the University of Denver Prison Arts Initiative concluded that arts programs can “invoke liberatory experiences for participants” (Littman & Sliva, 2021, as cited in Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.), and other studies report fewer depressive symptoms and a greater sense of self-respect and purpose among participants (Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.).

The Need for More Evidence

While peer-reviewed research conducted in carceral systems is thin, though growing, a meta-analysis of arts therapies in forensic settings, including 11 randomized or controlled trials, found improvements in psychiatric symptoms and in social and psychological functioning (Abbing et al., 2023). In a randomized trial with 200 men in a Chinese prison, group music therapy reduced anxiety and depression and raised self-esteem (Chen et al., 2016).

The punitive model assumes that people choose crime and that harsher consequences will deter them. Research offers little support for that assumption: compared with non-custodial sentences, imprisonment has a null or slightly criminogenic effect on reoffending (Nagin et al., 2009). Scholars and organizers including Angela Y. Davis (2003), Ruth Wilson Gilmore (2022), and Mariame Kaba (2021) call for moving resources away from prisons and toward the people and institutions that help communities thrive.

The arts are one of those investments. “Alternatives to incarceration, including restorative and transformative approaches, ask what people and communities need to heal,” Fix explains. “For many, creative expression is part of that answer, as an alternative to the traumatic carceral environment, though arts programming within prisons can also offer meaningful support where alternatives don't yet exist.” They give people a structured, safe outlet for processing difficult experiences, room to rehearse a new identity, and a way to contribute something others value.

The arts also help people who have been incarcerated speak for themselves. Ear Hustle, a podcast about life inside created at San Quentin State Prison by Earlonne Woods, who was then incarcerated there, and artist Nigel Poor, reached a national audience and was a 2020 Pulitzer Prize finalist (The Pulitzer Prizes, 2020).

The arts can be a powerful tool to support the social and emotional health of incarcerated individuals. For the men who learned to act at Sing Sing and then played themselves on screen, creative work was part of how they rebuilt their lives. Far more people leaving prison deserve the same chance.

~~~

Maya Lakshman, MPH, is a doctoral candidate at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where she uses neuroimaging, geospatial, and qualitative methods to understand the impacts of structural and interpersonal violence on development and mental health across the lifespan. She is a writer, educator, and researcher with an interest in translating evidence into equitable, justice-centered public health policy.

item.title: Why Does Everyone Else's Weight Loss Feel So Personal?
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Why Does Everyone Else's Weight Loss Feel So Personal?

How someone else's weight loss can make us question our own bodies.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Praising weight loss reinforces the belief that thinner bodies have more value than larger bodies.
  • Seeing others lose weight can bring back painful memories of dieting or eating disorder behaviors.
  • The growing use of GLP-1 medications can make it harder to escape pressure to lose weight.

A friend tells you she's lost 20 pounds. A coworker shows up looking noticeably smaller. Your sister mentions that she's started taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss. You recognize that what they do with their bodies is their decision, but before long, you're thinking about your own appearance. You start wondering whether you've gained weight, studying yourself in the mirror, or questioning what you ate that day. Nothing about your body has changed since yesterday, so why are you suddenly feeling dissatisfied with it?

Weight Loss Doesn't Happen in a Vacuum

Weight loss is so widely celebrated that congratulating someone for becoming thinner has become a normal and socially acceptable response. Yet weight loss can happen for many reasons, including illness, depression, stress, inadequate nourishment, or an eating disorder. Even when someone has intentionally lost weight and feels good about it, praising the change reinforces the idea that a smaller body is a better body.

We rarely consider what these compliments might mean to someone who later regains the weight. After hearing how wonderful they looked when they were thinner, they may worry that others now find them less attractive or assume they've let themselves go. Nobody has to make a negative comment about their weight gain for them to feel ashamed. The earlier praise has already communicated which version of their body was considered more desirable.

These messages also reinforce the stigma people with larger bodies face, whose appearance is often used to make assumptions about their health, behaviors, and self-discipline. We have become so accustomed to associating thinness with health and attractiveness, and have been told that everyone can and should control their weight and shape. These beliefs end up pathologizing the natural diversity of human bodies.

What Someone Else's Weight Loss Can Bring Up

I think there's more to these reactions than jealousy, particularly for people who have struggled with eating disorders or chronic dieting. Seeing someone else lose weight can bring back memories of when changing your body felt like the solution to so many things you were unhappy about.

Source: Clark Street Mercantile / Unsplash

Think about all the things you may have missed out on because you felt bad about your body. Perhaps you avoided swimming with friends because you didn't want to be seen in a bathing suit, made excuses not to go to parties because you felt uncomfortable with how you looked, or refused to buy clothes you liked until you went down two sizes. You kept promising yourself that you'd do these things once you were thinner. Looking back, there's sadness in recognizing how many experiences you missed while waiting to feel comfortable in your body.

For someone recovering from an eating disorder, watching another person receive praise for losing weight can bring back memories of the approval they once received. You may remember feeling accomplished when the number on the scale went down, even though maintaining that weight required behaviors that were harming you. It can be upsetting to miss those feelings, especially when you remember how miserable you were at the time.

Eating disorder recovery involves questioning beliefs about food, weight, and self-worth that are deeply embedded in our culture. Sometimes those old thoughts resurface, particularly when the people around you celebrate the very thing you've worked so hard to stop pursuing.

The GLP-1 Era Has Made Weight Loss Harder to Ignore

Talk about weight loss has always been difficult to avoid, but the widespread use of GLP-1 medications has brought even more of these conversations into everyday life. People share stories about medications, compare how much weight they've lost, and discuss changes in their appetites. Even a simple dinner can turn into a conversation about portion sizes or how little someone is eating.

Source: Kev Costello / Unsplash

In my work as a therapist specializing in eating disorders and body image distress, I hear how frustrating this has become for people who have spent years trying to improve their relationship with food. After working to become less preoccupied with eating and weight, they're surrounded by people discussing medications and the pursuit of smaller bodies. Some describe feeling pulled back into a way of thinking they've worked hard to leave behind.

GLP-1 medications have also changed how people think about losing weight. With weight loss increasingly presented as something that can be achieved through medication, those who have stopped pursuing it may begin questioning their decision. There's a growing sense that if changing your body is possible, you should at least consider it. For someone who has worked to accept their body, that pressure can be difficult to resist.

Remember What Dieting Was Actually Like

If hearing about someone else's weight loss makes you want to start dieting again, think about what your previous attempts to lose weight were actually like. Maybe you lost weight and felt good about yourself for a while, only to regain the weight, sometimes more than you initially lost. Each time, you blamed yourself for not having enough willpower or discipline and promised you'd do better with the next diet.

Weight regain is common, in part because our bodies respond to weight loss by increasing hunger and conserving energy. Yet when a diet fails to produce lasting results, people tend to blame themselves rather than question the diet. After years of losing and regaining weight, that repeated sense of failure can seriously affect how someone feels about themselves.

It's worth remembering what those years of dieting actually involved. Perhaps you constantly thought about food, felt guilty after eating, or judged yourself based on what the scale said that morning. If you've decided to stop dieting or are recovering from an eating disorder, you likely had good reasons for wanting something different for yourself. Another person's weight loss doesn't change those experiences.

Managing the Feelings That Come Up

It's understandable to feel uncomfortable when a friend talks about losing weight, especially if you find yourself comparing your appearance to hers. You might even feel envious of the attention she's receiving and then guilty for having those thoughts. Given how much importance our culture places on thinness, these reactions aren't surprising.

Sometimes the way to cope with those feelings and protect your eating disorder recovery is to first pay attention to what happens afterward. Are you checking your body more frequently, reconsidering foods you've been comfortable eating, or thinking about restarting a diet? Recognizing these changes early can help you avoid slipping back into behaviors you've worked to move away from.

It's also reasonable to limit conversations about dieting and weight loss. You can change the subject or tell someone, "I'm trying to spend less time thinking and talking about weight, so I'd rather hear about what else is going on in your life." You don't owe anyone a detailed explanation of your relationship with food or your body.

When Someone Else's Body Changes, Yours Doesn't Have to

We can't prevent other people from pursuing weight loss or control how much attention their changing bodies receive. But we can question why someone else's weight loss has become a reason to criticize our own appearance. You don't have to return to dieting, change how you eat, or become smaller simply because someone else has. Their body is theirs, and yours doesn't need to change in response.

item.title: Why Thinking Rationally Often Doesn’t Seem to Help
item.description:
Cognition

Why Thinking Rationally Often Doesn’t Seem to Help

Thinking rationally is often not the magic solution it is often presented to be.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Typical rational thinking by itself does not present any direction on what to do about situations.
  • In order to think in a truly full and useful rational way it is important to turn thinking inwards.
  • Deciding how situations fit with our meaning and purpose is essential for full and useful rational thinking.
  • When confronting emotional distress, think more about its fit with how you define meaning and purpose.

Thinking rationally is often presented as a magic answer to life’s problems. If we can just think more rationally and understand the reality of our world, then we will feel much better.

At least that’s what people say. But the truth is, just recognizing the reality of what is happening to us and around us often is not enough. We can understand clearly what is happening and still feel lousy about it.

Take the following example. A person recognizes that their job is no longer working for them. They go into work every day, put in the hours and feel absolutely terrible. After thinking about it, they realize that they hate their job. It may be that the work is no longer meaningful, they don’t feel like they are going anywhere, their boss is a tyrant, or a combination of all three. Coming to the conclusion, rationally, that the source of their distress is the meaninglessness or difficulty of their job can be useful.

But notice how recognizing reality does not guide the person on what to do here. It does not tell the person whether to leave their job, talk with their boss, or find some way to manage the problems the job presents. It also offers no guidance on how to handle the stress, as the person remains at the job even if they decide to look for a new one.

We often expect that if we just understand the reality of a situation, we will be able to deal with it or know what to do with it. But that is not the way reality actually works. Recognizing that something “is the way it is”, to quote an overused cliche, does not mean that we will know how to handle that reality.

Our experiences are ones where we all have to deal with the reality of our social world. But reality itself does not present information about what meaning we associate with it. Things happen, situations evolve, and people act as they do without these situations providing any clear guidance on how we are supposed to respond.

I once had a conversation with an expert in biological evolution who used a phrase that I still use today: “Evolution isn't good or bad, it just is.” I think about that phrase whenever I reflect on the fact that the world itself does not provide any clear indication of what things mean when they occur. All we know about the world is that things happen, and that things are the way they are, but knowing that rationally does not tell us what it means.

Rational thinking is a good starting place for handling reality effectively. But it is not enough. In order to effectively use rational information, you need to incorporate your own thinking about values and meaning.

In some ways, this is an extension of rational thinking. It is just rational thinking turned more inward. You move from asking “what facts do I know about what is happening here?” to “what facts do I know about how I define meaning and purpose?” Knowing those facts about how you want to live your life allows you to incorporate them into processing effectively what is happening to you and what is happening around you.

So, the solution is not to move away from thinking rationally. It is living your life more rationally. Living in a rational way does not mean you know the facts about what is happening to you and around you. It also means knowing:

  1. The facts about what you want out of life.
  2. What purpose you have in your life.
  3. How you want to use your limited time on Earth.
  4. Ways that you define meaning in your life.

Here are some important points to consider when trying to live your life in a more fully rational way

  1. Recognize that knowing the reality of the situation does not mean you necessarily know what to do with that information.
  2. Being able to state clearly what you find meaningful and important, major parts of thinking more fully rationally, helps you deal with the facts about what you are experiencing.
  3. Emotional distress can be a major factor related to thinking more rationally. Recognizing reality does not mean you will feel good about it. Distress can be a strong motivator for deciding more deeply what you think about a situation.
  4. Deciding what to do about a situation may mean you accept that you do not do anything (at least for now). Just accepting that reality bothers you while also acknowledging that you cannot change it can by itself be helpful.

item.title: You Don’t Have to Do Everything Yourself
item.description:
Self-Help

You Don’t Have to Do Everything Yourself

Why learning to accept help is a sign of strength.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Independence doesn’t mean doing everything on your own.
  • Asking for help doesn’t make us any less capable.
  • When we let someone help, we give them the opportunity to show they care.
Source: Priscilla Du Preez / Unsplash

When was the last time you were on a rollercoaster? Honestly, I can't remember the last time I was on one, although lately life itself has felt like a rollercoaster ride. Riding the highs, lows, and everything in between certainly keeps things interesting, even if some days it feels pretty challenging. But it's reminded me of something important: You don't have to do everything yourself.

This is not an easy thing for me to admit. I’ve always been fiercely independent. I've always been determined to figure things out myself. I struggle to ask for help because I hate the idea of inconveniencing anyone and, honestly, because it makes me feel weak and incapable. Yet, I know that's not true, not for me or for anyone else. Sometimes, we just need help.

That doesn't mean someone else has to completely take over and solve our problems for us. It could mean hearing a different perspective, getting some new ideas, or just being listened to. Or it could mean someone holds our hand and stands there with us. Whatever shape that help takes, it's OK to ask for it, even if it feels hard.

Most of our cultures place a lot of value on independence. Self-sufficiency, resilience, and the ability to keep going are all celebrated. We’re encouraged to take responsibility for our lives, solve our own problems, and not rely too heavily on anyone else. These are all useful qualities, but like with most things, they can be taken too far. That’s why asking for help can leave us feeling like failures. Yet, when I think about the people I love, I would never want them to feel they couldn't ask for my help. I would want them to tell me when things were difficult so I could show up for them. So why is it so hard to offer ourselves that same kindness?

Asking for Help Shows Strength

When I think about it, I believe asking for help is a sign of strength. It means we're vulnerable enough to admit that we don't have everything figured out. It means we're brave enough to acknowledge that perhaps we don’t want to do something alone. None of this makes us any less capable; it simply makes us human. And, if we look at research, accepting help can actually make us stronger humans. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found that feeling socially supported is associated with better mental and physical health. Maybe that's because knowing we're not facing a difficult situation alone can already make it feel more manageable.

To add to this, we can look at the perspective of the person offering the help. Think about how it feels when someone you care about lets you help them. You lend them a hand when they're overwhelmed, and you can see how much it helps them. It feels good to be there for them. So refusing help can actually deny someone who cares for you the opportunity to show they care.

Research has also explored this side of social support, with a 2017 review suggesting that providing care and support can benefit the person giving it as well as the person receiving it. This doesn’t mean we have to accept every offer of help, especially if we really don't feel like we need it. But maybe occasionally we underestimate how much people want to be there for us. I know I do. When we let someone help, we’re giving them the opportunity to do something meaningful, both for them and for us.

Independence Includes Recognising When You Need Support

Being independent doesn’t mean never needing anyone. It means recognising our limits and allowing others to help. After all, there’s no award for making life harder by insisting on doing everything alone (and even if there was, how silly would that be?!). Asking for help doesn’t make us any weaker. It simply means that while we can stand on our own two feet, sometimes we’d like someone to stand there with us.

I'm going to leave you with an excerpt from one of my favourite books, The Boy, the Mole, the Fox, and the Horse by Charlie Mackesy:

“What is the bravest thing you’ve ever said?” asked the boy.

“Help,” said the horse.

“Asking for help isn’t giving up,” said the horse. “It’s refusing to give up.”

item.title: How Pathological Narcissism Erodes the Best of Relationships
item.description:
Narcissism

How Pathological Narcissism Erodes the Best of Relationships

Life with a pathological narcissist is never very good; new research shows why.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • People high in vulnerable narcissism constantly seek assurance, leading them to lose faith in their partners.
  • New research shows how the rivalry dimension of narcissism can become the cause of this lack of faith.
  • Relationships with vulnerable narcissists may be salvageable by understanding the source of their rivalry.

Being able to trust your partner to want the best for you forms the bedrock of a close relationship. No one wants a romantic partner who constantly engages in sabotage and deception. So what happens when people discover that their partner turns out to be doing just that?

Consider Betty and Francis, who started dating a year ago, having met online. Betty always felt that Francis was a bit on the overly competitive side, turning everything into a battle for victory. If Betty succeeded at work on some small achievement, Francis refused to take it seriously. Betty decided to stick it out because Francis seems to need her there and often relies on her for support. But warning signs like these are making her think that maybe she’d better get out while she still can.

The Path to Destruction With a Pathological Narcissist

As pointed out in a new study by Saint Camillus International University’s Guyonne Rogier and colleagues (2026), “trust appears to be one of the most desired features in a partner.” They key component of trust, they go on to note, is faith, or the confidence that a partner will remain caring and helpful regardless of what may happen in the future. It’s this uncertainty factor that could prove to be the hardest for narcissistic individuals to accept. But it’s not just any narcissistic individual; vulnerable narcissists should be particularly unhappy with the uncertainty factor. They don’t want to risk any possible rejection or disappointment from their partner.

Narcissism alone, even the vulnerable form, isn’t the only factor that can destroy faith and, hence, relationships. Rogier et al. point out that highly narcissistic people approach relationships from the two dimensions of admiration and rivalry. They are afraid of being outdone by their partner, because this would threaten their sense of worth. The activation of feelings of rivalry sets off the chain of reactions that ultimately leads faith to fall by the wayside.

Testing the Rivalry as the Destroyer of Relationships

The Italian authors tested this potential set of mechanisms by building a model that started with vulnerable narcissism as the origin of feelings of rivalry. In turn, rivalry toward the partner would lead, the model predicted, to the outcome of loss of faith in the romantic partner. Although this was a correlational study, the authors were able to test their model using controlled statistical modeling.

The online sample of more than 4,000 Italian adults (average age of 32 years) completed a set of standard personality questionnaires. Faith was measured with items such as “Even if I don’t know how my partner will react, I feel comfortable telling him/her anything about myself, even the things I am ashamed of” (reverse-scored). To measure vulnerable narcissism, the authors used the corresponding scale from the Narcissism Personality Inventory, with items such as “Sometimes I avoid people because I fear they will disappoint me.” Finally, rivalry was assessed with three subscales from the Narcissism Admiration and Rivalry Questionnaire (NARQ): Devaluation (“Other people are worth nothing”), Supremacy (“I want my rivals to fail”), and Aggressiveness (“I get annoyed when someone steals the attention from me”).

Consistent with the authors’ prediction, grandiose but not vulnerable narcissism predicted lack of faith in the partner. Grandiose narcissists may rival their partners, but they feel confident in how “magnificent and unique” they are, which should ensure their partner’s “love and devotion.” Vulnerable narcissists, anxiously attached to their partners, don’t have this same level of confidence in their ability. This leads the narcissistic rivalry to emerge, much as has happened to Betty and Francis.

Tracing the trajectory of relationships for people high in vulnerable narcissism from the study’s results reinforces this idea. In a good relationship, faith develops over time as the partners become less fearful of rejection even if they show their weak side. In relationships with vulnerable narcissists, rivalry builds over time. They start to devalue and distrust their partner the more they reveal their flaws and limitations. The rivalry becomes increasingly aggressive as a means of self-protection.

Stopping Rivalry’s Progressive Effects on Faith

If you’ve been in a situation like Betty’s, you can understand the push and pull that she might be experiencing. You can feel bad for a vulnerable narcissist whose precarious sense of self seems to need constant reinforcing. But when this person starts to attack you, this tries your patience. It can even make you start to question your own self-worth.

Pinpointing the problem in the maladaptive quality of narcissistic rivalry could provide you with important insights. The vulnerable narcissist may not “want” to be nasty, but may be unable to control the aggressive attempts to put you down. The flip side of rivalry is admiration. The grandiose narcissist may have too much of this feeling of self-satisfaction and superiority, but the vulnerable narcissist may need a bit more.

Returning to the primary purpose of the study, it can also be helpful to think about the faith dimension. A person high in vulnerable narcissism never feels certain of the future, which includes the certainty that a romantic partner will remain faithful. This can lead to endless worry but also endless attempts to win any battle for superiority.

To sum up, life with a pathological narcissist is never very pleasant. If you care about this person, though, understanding how rivalry breeds lack of faith can help you intervene before the dynamics take a toll on your relationship.
