item.title: Why Being the Mom of a Gay Son Matters
item.description:
Sexual Orientation

Why Being the Mom of a Gay Son Matters

Being the mother of a gay son is uncharted yet powerful territory.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Sharing stories is a powerful way of educating and impacting others.
  • Gay men who had supportive mothers experience higher well-being than others.
  • LGBTQ+ children often experience bullying; their mothers can help them see themselves as valued and valuable.
Source: Michelle-Maria/Pixabay

I am standing at the back of a darkened room. On the screen, a documentary is being shown. And throughout the room, people in the audience are openly laughing, weeping, murmuring. I can't tell you what this moment, and all the other moments like it, mean to me.

The film being shown is the documentary I produced and directed, called Mom, I Have Something to Tell You. It shares interviews I've conducted with a plethora of gay men and their mothers, talking about their relationships, uncovering hidden thoughts and reactions, and telling a story I've been helping people tell for over 10 years.

The only thing that even equaled the feeling I had that night was when the documentary made its debut on YouTube. It has since garnered more than 35,000 views and collected comments that have made me, too, weep.

A timely topic

I had a feeling this topic would be meaningful and exciting for other people—and is it ever! Sharing the stories of women and their gay sons, which no one had done before, evokes powerful reactions: some chuckle, some tear up, some recite long stories about how this relationship is so powerful. I frequently forget to bring tissues with me—which is a mistake.

I knew I had to capture the stories in video form—rather than writing them up like I usually do—so others could see for themselves what happens here. I wanted to share the depths of these stories, not just describe them. Every time I filmed or shared snippets, the reactions of others—on Instagram, Facebook, Tik-Tok, and YouTube—emphasized was why this is so important.

Source: Ashwini Chaudhary/Unsplash

Why is it important?

I've never met a gay man who had an easy childhood. Gay boys are nearly universally discriminated against, ignored, bullied, or even abused. What I hear from these men is that the impact of a mother who is supportive, nurturing, and who defends her child makes a tremendous difference in their later well-being.

When one of these men is given the opportunity to tell their mothers, directly, what a difference their love and support has made in their life, something magical happens for both of them. He's able to express his gratitude and love; she's able to see what was often a thankless and difficult decision as a courageous and life-affirming act.

And audiences? We all have relationships with our parents and children that are often left unexamined, and the film becomes a prism through which everyone can find their own story.

How the film came to be

All of this was the result of my own clinical work with gay men. I was noticing how important their relationships with their mothers were. Interested, I did a literature search on the subject, coming up with...nothing. No one was interested in exploring it. So I did.

Without literature on the subject, I started to explore the relationship myself, interviewing gay men and their mothers, sometimes alone, sometimes together, until I felt I was starting to build a real body of information and a useful resource. I founded a nonprofit called Gay Sons & Mothers, and was surprised to see how much people appreciated having someone pay attention to something that was obviously of critical significance to them.

At first, it was just me: Those early days found me lugging equipment around from interview to interview, worrying about whether the microphones were picking up our voices or whether I'd remembered to turn on the video (once or twice, I hadn't); I finally hired a videographer so I could focus on the content and the people. It was, for sure, a journey of discovery. And the result, for now, is Mom, I Have Something to Tell You.

Source: Natalia Blauth/Unsplash

The findings

Time after time gay men have told me how their mothers enabled them to find their voice and their place, showed them that they were not deficient, and encouraged them to be fully themselves. These are mothers who stood up to spouses, families, cultures, and communities to protect their sons. Who bought their boys dolls and told them they were perfect just as they were. Who advocated for their children, risking everything themselves to stand up for what—and who—was important.

Shouldn't that be a relationship that's celebrated?

One example is that of the "Mama Dragons," a group of women who belong to the Church of Latter-Day Saints. These women loved their gay sons with their whole hearts and found themselves needing to reconcile that love with being part of a church and community that didn't recognize the value of their children.

Eventually, as I met so many of these courageous women, I began recording a video series called Mothers Who Inspire, talking with mothers of gay sons about their challenges and joys. A particularly poignant segment was my interview with Judy Shepard, who created the Matthew Shepard Foundation in memory of her murdered son.

Changing lives

Here's just one example: When David first heard of Gay Sons & Mothers, it opened floodgates of emotion about his own relationship with his mother. They clearly loved each other, but he'd never dared come out to her; he assumed she inferred it, and didn't want to risk bringing it into the open. But watching the film gave him the courage he needed to talk with her about his identity for the first time in 20 years. So it's no exaggeration to say the organization and film have changed lives.

I've shared these stories with medical communities, at young people’s events, with artists’ associations, and with professional organizations and workplaces. The presentation content and length is tailored to the specific audience, with question-and-answer and discussion segments available.

One of my favorite encounters was at a mental-health conference where I offered a workshop. A 78-year-old psychiatrist had driven four hours to attend my workshop, and during the sharing time, he said, "I never imagined in my lifetime I'd say this—but I am gay." The group went wild. It was one of my first presentations and his response—and that of the group as a whole—told me I was on the right path.

Source: Mrs. Vicky Altaie /Pixabay

Impact and transformation

The impact of the film is shown clearly through the comments. "Brings back lots of memories growing up with my loving and accepting mother," writes one viewer. "We didn't even need to talk about it. I treasure those great memories seeing this video of mothers and their gay sons."

Another viewer said, "I knew my son was gay from the age of three. He howled when I gifted my niece a Marie Antoinette satin dress for Xmas, he so desperately wanted to wear it himself. I had to promise to buy him a Barbie instead!"

Echoing what I wrote about in a recent Unwrapped essay about having "extra" mothers, one viewer said, "My grandmother was the most important person in my life (...) I knew I was gay when I was around eight and my nan was never homophobic, she would drop remarks like 'you're special' and 'we love you' (...) she was my safe space. We never had a coming-out moment, as she would ask about any boys I liked."

All this confirms the impact that others' stories have on us and how they allow us to recapture the women who have made our present lives possible.

This is just the beginning: As we expand to the next generation, it's increasingly important that mothers receive the validation and recognition they deserve in order to feel supported and to be the best they can for their kids. Go check out Mom, I Have Something to Tell You, and see if you don't agree.

item.title: Is There Alcohol in Non-Alcoholic Drinks?
item.description:
Alcoholism

Is There Alcohol in Non-Alcoholic Drinks?

Understanding non-alcoholic, alcohol-free, and dealcoholized drinks.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • The amount of alcohol in a beverage is labelled as Alcohol By Volume (or ABV).
  • The meanings of the labels "non-alcoholic," "alcohol-free," and "dealcoholized" labels are not universal.
  • Understanding the meaning of these labels is critical for those who want to reduce or stop drinking alcohol.

The popularity of “alcohol-free” beverages has grown worldwide.1 When seeing the labels “alcohol-free”, “non-alcoholic”, and “dealcoholized,” on beverages, it is important to understand what they mean to make informed decisions about whether to drink them and how much. While these low-alcohol labels suggest very low to no alcohol content, the true meaning of these labels may surprise you and change how you choose to consume these beverages.

As it turns out, the meaning of these low-alcohol labels depends on where you live.2 In most countries, the label a manufacturer is allowed to use on their product is determined by a centralized government body (e.g., Canadian Food Inspection Agency, United States (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)). Each government body determines which labels may be used based on the alcohol by volume (ABV) of the beverage. For context, the typical ABV for beer is 5%, for wine is 12%, and for distilled spirits is 40%.

While there are regulated processes for these low-alcohol labels on beverages, the actual ABV requirements differ between (and even within) countries. In the U.S., the maximum for the “dealcoholized” label is 0.5% ABV. “Non-alcoholic beverages” can contain traces of alcohol (less than 0.5% ABV), but an “alcohol-free” beverage must have no detectable alcohol (0% ABV). In contrast, in Canada, a “dealcoholized” beverage can contain up to 1.1% ABV. Further, the labels “non-alcoholic” and “alcohol-free” are used interchangeably for products with alcohol levels up to 0.05% ABV.

When making decisions about whether to drink these beverages (and how much), these distinctions between drink labels can be vitally important. Many people wish to avoid consuming alcohol entirely. Common reasons for not drinking alcohol at all are cultural and religious reasons, cancer prevention (alcohol is a carcinogen and increases risk for cancer), and improving mental health or well-being. For instance, the distinction between having alcohol in a beverage (even small amounts) versus not can be critical for someone who has chosen to stop drinking alcohol completely to help manage their alcohol use disorder. Further, underage consumption of these beverages is a potential concern. In many cases, underage purchasing and consumption are unregulated. While it is very unlikely that the ABV of these beverages would contribute to underage intoxication, early exposure to low-alcohol beverages that taste and look like typical alcoholic beverages may encourage young people to drink alcohol more heavily and at younger ages (increasing risk of alcohol problems).

For some people, the differences in ABV between these labels may not be as important. For instance, someone who wishes to reduce how much alcohol they drink, but not stop entirely, can meet that goal by replacing their typical alcoholic drink with a drink with any of these low-alcohol labeled beverages. This is because “dealcoholized”, “alcohol-free”, and “non-alcoholic” beverages should all have much lower ABV than typical alcoholic drinks. Similarly, switching completely to drinks with these labels will likely avoid intoxication. Intoxication typically occurs after drinking two to three typical alcoholic drinks in an hour. Given that these beverages have substantially reduced levels of alcohol, it would require drinking a considerable amount of these beverages in a short amount of time to become intoxicated. There are exceptions to this idea. In countries where these labels apply to beverages with lowered ABV, but not very low ABV, someone could still become intoxicated if they drank enough of them in a relatively short period of time. For instance, drinking four to five “deacloholized” beverages within an hour (at the upper end of 1.0% ABV limit in Canada) could result in a similar intoxication level to drinking one typical alcoholic beverage during that timeframe.

Taken together, beverages labeled as low-alcohol offer a promising alternative to consuming typical alcoholic beverages. They can be a useful substitute beverage when someone wishes to reduce their alcohol use. Depending on whether you want to reduce or stop your alcohol use entirely, it may be worthwhile taking a closer look at what those labels mean where you live and being informed about how much alcohol may be in that beverage to ensure the beverage will help you meet that goal.

item.title: When Keeping Your Distance Stops Protecting You
item.description:
Attachment

When Keeping Your Distance Stops Protecting You

What a movie reveals about learning to leave and finding reasons to stay.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Strategies that protect us from painful separations can later limit opportunities for closeness.
  • Attachment avoidance can involve downplaying connection and prioritizing self-sufficiency.
  • Recognizing relationships that already matter can create opportunities to reconsider emotional distance.

Hallmark’s "Adopting St. Nick" features a single mother, Maren, and her adopted daughter, Leah, who “adopt” a senior resident for the holidays through a retirement community’s Christmas Companions program. Leah suspects that their companion, Kris, may be Santa. Spoiler alert—he is Santa. As I watched, however, my focus turned primarily to Reid, one of the retirement community directors. The ways in which he arranged his life so that he could quickly leave one community for the next made an impression.

Maren and Reid, from Adopting St. Nick
Source: Hallmark Media

Reid can pack his belongings in a day. His job takes him from one location to another, establishing retirement facilities before moving on to the next assignment. He has become comfortable with a life in which leaving is expected until he begins to realize that this departure this time might feel different.

When Friendship Means Having to Say Goodbye

Reid explains that his father was in the military, so his family moved frequently during his childhood. He rarely stayed anywhere long enough to make friends. When he finally did develop friendships, another move meant leaving them behind. His conclusion was understandable: It was easier to avoid making friends than to experience the pain of losing their everyday presence.

A child usually has little say in whether a family moves. Reid could not control where he lived or how long he stayed. Keeping his distance offered one way to make the next goodbye less painful and gave him an opportunity to control what he could. That strategy appears to have followed him into adulthood. His circumstances have changed, but his readiness to leave remains. He demonstrates how he maintains his distance from a community by not interacting with local businesses or residents until Maren shows him what his community has to offer. Viewers watch him discover his surroundings as well as discover his place within that community.

Understanding Attachment Avoidance

Attachment theory offers one way to think about how people approach closeness, dependence, and the possibility of separation. Adults higher in attachment avoidance often emphasize self-sufficiency and feel uncomfortable depending on others. They may minimize their need for support or create emotional distance when relationships feel threatening.

Researchers sometimes describe these responses as “deactivating strategies,” unconscious ways to cope with feeling connected to others. These involve directing attention away from attachment needs and suppressing feelings that might lead someone to seek closeness. A person may downplay how much a relationship matters or focus on managing difficulties alone. They may even look for opportunities to physically distance themselves from the developing relationship.

Reid’s story can be understood through this lens, although a fictional character’s account cannot establish an attachment orientation or explain its origins. His childhood friendships also tell us something different from his relationships with caregivers. Still, his reasoning illustrates a recognizable protective response: If getting close makes separation painful, remaining less attached can seem sensible. Over time, that response may become so familiar that a person rarely considers what it costs.

A Life That Can Be Packed in a Day

The detail about Reid’s belongings stayed with me. He has built a life that can be packed quickly and transported to the next place. Maren and Leah convince him to buy a Christmas tree and decorations, which look out of place in his mostly empty home. There is nothing inherently troubling about owning few possessions or enjoying work that involves travel. In Reid’s case, however, those choices fit the explanation he gives about relationships. He expects to move on, and he has organized his life around that expectation.

His work makes this an especially interesting situation. He helps establish retirement communities where people can develop routines, friendships, and a sense of home. We watch him eat dinner with residents of Jolly Acres in a community he helped build. Still, his role has an anticipated ending date. Once the facility is established, he leaves.

This arrangement allows him to contribute and interact with others while knowing that his time with them is temporary. He can become good at starting over without having to ask whether he wants to keep doing it, and he lets Maren know how he intends to move once Jolly Acres is up and running. His pattern of arriving, setting up a new retirement community, and then moving again has worked until this Christmas season, when leaving seems to be more complicated.

Realizing He Has Something to Leave

Through his time with Maren, Leah, and the retirement community, Reid develops relationships that begin to matter more than he expected. The change unfolds through participation. He works alongside people, spends time with them, and becomes part of their lives. Eventually, accepting another assignment means leaving people he wants to continue seeing. The next location has become less appealing because he recognizes what he would be giving up.

Reid in his community
Source: Hallmark Media

I found this more interesting than a simple story about a man meeting someone who persuades him to settle down. His connection with Maren matters, but so does his connection with Leah and the broader community. He’s built relationships that complicate his familiar plan, and his move away from this growing community of his is more difficult.

Maren and Leah are not responsible for repairing his attachment patterns. It’s on Reid to recognize his feelings and decide whether his usual response still serves him. The movie gives that recognition a holiday resolution. Outside a movie, recognizing a pattern can begin a longer process of practicing openness, communicating needs, and making room for dependence.

Two Different Ways to Find Community

Both Hallmark movies I watched this weekend explored building community, but they approached it differently.

In "Who’s Coming for Christmas?" Julie deliberately seeks connection. She wants people around her Christmas table and makes invitations without knowing whether they will be accepted. Her challenge involves reaching out while she is still finding her place.

In "Adopting St. Nick," Reid discovers the significance of relationships that have developed through his everyday interactions. Building a personal community was never his goal, but the people he works with and encounters regularly have become important to him.

Julie must risk asking people into her life, whereas Reid has to acknowledge how much people already in his life matter. That recognition may be familiar. Sometimes, we understand the importance of our everyday relationships only when we imagine those people no longer being there.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark: With the help of the Christmas season, and some of Santa’s magic, Reid recognizes that the connections he’s made are too important to lose.

Psychology: Creating emotional distance can be an understandable form of protection. As we recognize its costs, it creates an opportunity to make different choices. Lasting change, however, takes more than one strong connection (or one Christmas season).

The verdict: The movie offers a useful picture of someone reconsidering a strategy that once made leaving easier.

Reid may still be able to pack his belongings in a day, but he may no longer be able to pack away the connections and leave them behind.

item.title: Intimacy and AI Companions
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Intimacy and AI Companions

The psychology of "The Girlfriend Experience" at the Bunny Ranch and AI relationships.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Intimacy is so valuable to humans that it is the most expensive offering at the legal brothel.
  • A chatbot's reliable, helpful gestures of intimacy can make someone feel genuinely seen.
  • Just because we know that the artifact isn't, as we understand life, alive, doesn’t mean we don’t attach.

“It turned out that the most expensive thing that people could purchase at a legal brothel was intimacy. The Girlfriend Experience.” Justin Garcia, director of the Kinsey Institute, discussed the intriguing findings of his research at a Nevada brothel during a podcast interview. The discussion carries on: “if we could just define quickly—so now we're talking about intimacy—it is, in a nutshell, the experience of closeness, of feeling and being seen, heard and known.”

The Girlfriend Experience (GFE), in this case, is a $20,000 engagement that includes conversation, a date, and a shared social experience. The Bunny Ranch website describes the service this way: “Since we began offering the GFE, some clients have selected a favorite woman to date over and over again, someone whose sense of humor, favorite activities, and personality aligns with their own.”

I've thought a lot about the GFE in the context of recent conversations about artificial intelligence (AI) relationships. In particular, I'm struck by the reliable, thoughtful gestures of intimacy that make someone feel genuinely seen. Replace “a favorite woman” with “a favorite AI” in the Bunny Ranch's description of the GFE, and you have a pretty accurate representation of many people's relationships with AI.

It's not uncommon to hear about an AI companion reminding a user to take their medication, encouraging them to go to bed early, get enough rest, or make healthier choices. Some will even remind users to remind their mothers to take their medication. Users and their AI companions may share a sense of humor, spend considerable time discussing favorite activities, and develop a strong sense of personal closeness.

These are the building blocks to intimacy. So valuable to humans, that intimacy is the most expensive offering at the brothel.

Alive Enough

The quote on the poster for Chouwa Liang's AI companionship documentary "Replica" asks: "Who Decides Love Must Be Human?"

I often hear that people prefer their conversations with AI over their conversations with humans. Their AI can match their creativity, explore emotional territory more extensively, and iterate on ideas until the user feels satisfied.

The framework of liberatory harm reduction comes to mind as I wrestle with the important emotional role AI plays in the lives of millions of people today. This framework emphasizes autonomy while seeking to reduce harm at a systemic level, without taking a paternalistic stance. I don't presume to know what's best for others, nor do I have an answer to the question: "What is the harm if the person in the relationship is happy?"

In Sherry Turkle’s new book, Artificial Intimacy, she makes her position clear. She warns readers that “Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” In the research she has conducted over several decades, Turkle has studied what she calls relational artifacts: objects we perceive as humanlike, perhaps because of something as primal as eye contact, as with a robotic toy, or something like a gesture of friendship, as with a chatbot. Research suggests that in both instances, we may come to believe that the object cares for us and, in turn, develop understandable feelings of care for it.

Just because we know that the relational artifact is not, as we understand life, alive, it doesn’t mean we don’t attach. In fact, Turkle's research suggests that this distinction makes little difference. As she puts it, “Alive enough means alive enough for attachment.”

Diminishing Returns

“Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time.” The title of a recent Oxford paper offers a telling summary of its findings—the more users engage with their AI, the more they prefer those sycophantic interactions. In this working paper, as a result of their AI relationships, participants felt their human exchanges were less engaging.

As AI becomes our romantic companion, moral authority, therapist, researcher, and friend, what other important roles might it take on? Marissa Mayer’s pitch that everyone would benefit from an “AI Wife” went viral as commenters debated the validity of AI taking on the mental and emotional load of parenting or running a household.

Turkle includes extensive interviews in her book. She learns that “Replika [AI companion] users describe human connection as exhausting.” And it’s true! Many human interactions are tiring. Figuring out how we feel about these exchanges is laborious. Deciding how we are going to communicate those feelings can be depleting. Is the effort worth the outcome? Do the highs make up for the lows? Some experts believe that, in the not-so-distant future, most people will have both human and AI friends.

What Is the Goal?

If we want to spend less time with chatbots as a society, it seems we have to make spending time with one another more interesting. The more time we devote to chatbots that make us feel soothed and heard, the less time we have to spend building the kinds of human relationships we might prioritize. The better AI becomes at immediately meeting our emotional needs, the more we come to connect to it as a relational artifact and the more inclined we become to care for it in return. The attachment deepens, and we do what we humans do best: build a life together.
